claim.pdf_says: 8.4.3.13.2 General format, 8.4.3.13.3 Syntax rules and 8.4.3.13.4 General rules are printed at the same heading rank as 8.4.3.14.1 General on the same page (identical size and weight; all are fourth-level subsections of 8.4.3).
claim.markdown_says: Same page: `## 8.4.3.13.2 General format`, `## 8.4.3.13.3 Syntax rules`, `## 8.4.3.13.4 General rules` (level 2) but `### 8.4.3.14.1 General` (level 3) - the four-level headings of 8.4.3.13 are promoted to the same markdown level as the three-level section headings.
claim.why_it_matters: Promoted headings make 8.4.3.13.2-.4 siblings of 8.4.3.13 itself rather than its children, so a generated table of contents and any heading-based navigation misrepresent the section tree. NOTE: this is systemic, not local to page 172 - the same promotion occurs for 8.4.3.11.2-.4, 8.4.3.12.1-.4, 8.4.3.13.1, 8.4.3.14.2-.4, 8.4.3.15.2-.3 and (on page 306 of this batch) 11.9.10.1. Fix it as one sweep, not page by page.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED - no content discrepancy exists between the PDF and the transcription. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING. All five headings printed on page 172 are present in page-172.md with their clause numbers and titles verbatim: `## 8.4.3.13.2 General format` (l.7), `## 8.4.3.13.3 Syntax rules` (l.18), `## 8.4.3.13.4 General rules` (l.29), `## 8.4.3.14 LINAGE-COUNTER` (l.48), `### 8.4.3.14.1 General` (l.51). The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer; the sole difference is the count of '#' characters, which is markdown presentation markup the PDF does not encode at all. (2) THE PDF EVIDENCE IS NON-PROBATIVE AND PROVES TOO MUCH. I measured the rendered page (300 dpi, spec_p172.png) by row-ink profile and then inspected the cropped glyphs directly (headings_stack.png). Cap heights: 8.4.3.13.2 = 34 px, 8.4.3.13.4 = 34 px, 8.4.3.14 = 33 px, 8.4.3.14.1 = 34 px (8.4.3.13.3 measures 44 px only because 'Syntax rules' carries a 'y' descender). All five are the same bold serif at the same size. Critically, that includes the FOUR-component heading `8.4.3.14 LINAGE-COUNTER`, which is printed at exactly the same size and weight as the five-component `8.4.3.14.1 General`. ISO's typography gives deep subclause headings one uniform rank; it draws no visual distinction between clause depths anywhere on this page. So the claim's inference rule - 'printed at the same size and weight therefore the same markdown level' - would equally condemn `## 8.4.3.14` / `### 8.4.3.14.1`, the very pairing the claim holds up as CORRECT. A criterion that convicts the reference case cannot convict the accused case. The printed page simply cannot adjudicate markdown heading depth. (3) NO MEANING IS CHANGED. The section hierarchy is carried unambiguously by the dotted clause numbers themselves ('8.4.3.13.2' states its own parentage), and those numbers are transcribed exactly. A reader or a tool keyed on clause numbers recovers the identical tree. (4) THE UNDERLYING OBSERVATION, restated honestly, is a markdown-INTERNAL style inconsistency, not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy - and it is far broader and more arbitrary than the claim's own list. In specs/ISO_COBOL.md the level convention is unstable throughout this whole region, for four-component headings as well as five: `## 8.4.3.1` vs `### 8.4.3.3` vs `## 8.4.3.4` vs `### 8.4.3.9`; five-component headings appear at `##` (8.4.3.11.2), `###` (8.4.3.4.1, 8.4.3.14.1) and `####` (8.4.3.3.1, 8.4.3.9.1). Normalizing that is a global cosmetic tidy of the transcription's own markup with no PDF counterpart, and it belongs in a style-normalization pass rather than the PDF reconciliation ledger, where it would falsely record the standard as having been transcribed with lost content.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. Every heading on page 172 is present with its clause number and title verbatim; only the markdown '#' depth differs, and the PDF encodes no heading depth to differ from - measured at 300 dpi, all five headings including the four-component `8.4.3.14 LINAGE-COUNTER` and the five-component `8.4.3.14.1 General` print in identical bold serif at identical cap height (33-34 px). What genuinely exists is an internal markup-style inconsistency in specs/ISO_COBOL.md, whose heading levels do not track clause-number depth consistently anywhere in section 8.4.3 (four-component headings appear at both `##` and `###`; five-component headings at `##`, `###` and `####`). If that is worth fixing, fix it as a whole-file markup normalization derived from clause-number depth - not as a reconciliation finding against the PDF.
